longForm.title: The Siege of Badajoz, 1812: Forty Attempts on the Breach
longForm.excerpt: On the night of 6 April 1812, Wellington's army made forty separate attempts to cross the breaches at Badajoz. All forty failed. The fortress fell anyway — through the castle, through the bastion of San Vincente, and through losses that no rational military calculus would have predicted.
paragraphs: The breaches at Badajoz were ready by the evening of 6 April 1812. Three of them: the Trinidad breach, the Santa María breach, and a smaller one near the bastion of San Vincente. Wellington knew what his engineers were telling him. He also knew that General Armand Philippon knew, and that Philippon had spent the previous three weeks mining the approaches, setting chevaux-de-frise — iron bars fitted with sword blades — across the breach openings, and flooding the ditch in front of the walls. This was the third time British forces had tried to take Badajoz. The first two attempts, in 1811, had failed. Wellington ordered the assault for midnight.

Badajoz controlled the southern corridor between Portugal and Spain. Whoever held it held the gateway. For Wellington's Army, operating in the Peninsula since 1808, the fortress had become something more than a strategic objective — it had become an institutional problem. The 1811 sieges had cost lives and credibility. The French garrison under Philippon was not large, approximately 5,000 men, but Badajoz was a Vauban-designed fortress, modernized and well-maintained, and Philippon was a competent engineer-officer who understood exactly what the terrain gave him. Wellington had artillery, but not enough heavy pieces. He had a siege train that arrived late and was lighter than the operation required. He had the Army, which was willing.

The assault parties for the Trinidad and Santa María breaches were formed from the Light Division and the 4th Division — the best formations in the army, assigned the worst task. These were the forlorn hopes and the storming parties, volunteers and pressed men both. They knew what they were walking into. The breaches had been observed from the forward sap heads for days. Everyone could see the iron spikes set across the crests. Everyone knew the ditch was twelve feet deep and flooded. Wellington did not speak to them beforehand. There was nothing useful to say.

The assault began close to midnight on 6 April. The stormers moved forward from the trenches and almost immediately began dying. The French had wired lanterns to the breach crests; when the assault started, they lit them, and the breach faces were suddenly illuminated against the darkness. The men attacking the Trinidad breach ran into the chevaux-de-frise, fell into the ditch, tried to scramble up the far wall, and were met with grenades, shells, and musket fire from defenders who had prepared their positions for exactly this moment. Forty separate attempts were made on the Trinidad breach alone over the course of that night. All forty failed. The carnage at the foot of the walls was, by later accounts, something beyond what even veteran soldiers of the Peninsular War had seen before.

While the main assault was failing at the breaches, Lieutenant General Thomas Picton's 3rd Division escalated a diversionary attack on the castle — a near-vertical masonry face on the northeastern side of the town. Picton had no breach. His men brought ladders. The ladders were too short by several feet in places, and the first attempts were thrown back. Then, in one of those unplanned moments that determine outcomes, a section of wall was found where the scaling ladders could be extended by having the lead men stand on each other's shoulders. The 3rd Division got over. The fighting on the castle ramparts was close and violent in the dark, but Picton's men secured a foothold before the main breaches had been crossed. Picton himself was wounded during the assault, though he remained in the field.

Simultaneously, Major General James Leith's 5th Division attacked the bastion of San Vincente at the southwestern corner of the walls — an escalade using ladders and crowbars against a section of fortification that was not breached and had not been the primary target. Leith's men got over. By approximately 0400 on the morning of 7 April, British troops held the castle and the San Vincente bastion. Philippon, who had been directing the defense of the main breaches and was unaware that both flanks had collapsed, withdrew to the San Cristóbal fort across the Guadiana River with what remained of his garrison. He surrendered the following morning. The French garrison had held the breaches all night, successfully. They lost the fortress anyway.

What happened next is not well covered in Wellington's dispatches. The army broke into the town. British soldiers — men who had watched comrades die by the hundreds over the course of one night — spent the following thirty-six hours looting, drinking, and committing violence against the civilian population of Badajoz. The scale of the disorder was beyond what the officer corps could contain by conventional means. Wellington issued orders. The orders were not obeyed. It required the erection of a gallows in the town square and the threat of summary execution before discipline was restored. Wellington was reportedly seen weeping when he rode through the streets. He did not put his emotional state on the record, and later accounts of that moment must be treated as at least partially constructed.

The assault cost the British army approximately 3,713 casualties at the breaches alone in the hours of night fighting on 6 April. Total siege casualties across the full operation ran to approximately 4,760 killed and wounded. The French garrison suffered approximately 1,500 casualties, with the survivors becoming prisoners of war. Philippon was wounded twice. He had done everything correctly: the defense of Badajoz on the night of 6 April 1812 was a competent performance against overwhelming odds, and it succeeded in its immediate tactical objective. The fortress fell because Wellington's army absorbed losses that no rational military calculus would have predicted it could sustain and kept sending men at the wall. That is not a doctrine. It is a fact about what the army was capable of, and at what cost.

shortForm.title: Salamanca, 1812: Wellington's Forty-Minute Victory
shortForm.excerpt: On 22 July 1812, Wellington spotted a gap in Marmont's line and attacked. The decisive phase of the Battle of Salamanca lasted approximately forty minutes. The French Army of Portugal lost 14,000 men and its commander.
paragraphs: The morning of 22 July 1812 had been a war of marches. Wellington's Anglo-Portuguese army and Marshal Auguste Marmont's Army of Portugal had been maneuvering for position in the rolling terrain south of Salamanca for days, each commander seeking an opening that did not quite materialize. Then, at approximately 1700 hours, Wellington saw what he was looking for from the heights of Las Torres. Marmont's left wing — two divisions under General Thomières — was moving along the road to Alba de Tormes and had become separated from the rest of the French army. The gap between divisions was real and widening. Wellington is reported to have put down whatever he was eating and remarked to his staff that Marmont was lost. He ordered the 3rd Division forward immediately.

Marmont had made the error that Wellington could exploit. Thomières's two divisions were strung out, moving away from mutual support, with their left flank exposed to the ridge line that Wellington's force occupied. The 3rd Division under Edward Pakenham struck them from the northwest in a hammer blow while the 4th and 5th Divisions and the cavalry of General John Le Marchant struck the French center. Thomières's force disintegrated. Marmont himself was struck by shell fragments early in the action; his arm was shattered and he was removed from the field before the full consequences of his order became clear. His successor, General Bonnet, was also wounded within minutes, creating a command vacuum at the worst possible moment in the battle.

The decisive phase lasted approximately forty minutes. French casualties over the course of the day ran to approximately 14,000 killed, wounded, and captured — including the loss of two eagles. Wellington's losses were approximately 5,000. The Army of Portugal retreated north toward Burgos in disorder, effectively ending French offensive capacity in Spain for the remainder of the campaign season. Wellington entered Madrid on 12 August 1812, the first Allied entry into the Spanish capital since the war began. Salamanca demonstrated that Wellington could conduct aggressive offensive operations on ground of his choosing, not merely defend prepared positions. It was, in the judgment of many subsequent historians including Charles Oman, the finest of his tactical performances in the Peninsula.

onThisDay.headline: Napoleon Bonaparte Arrives on Elba, Beginning His First Exile
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1814, Napoleon Bonaparte arrived on the island of Elba, beginning his exile following his abdication on 11 April under the Treaty of Fontainebleau. He was granted sovereignty over the island and a pension; he would escape ten months later, landing in southern France on 1 March 1815 and beginning the Hundred Days campaign that ended at Waterloo.
